title: Key concepts: units and equations
subtitle: SI units, prefixes, standard form, converting compound units and rearranging equations
lede: Topic 1 is short — units, prefixes, converting, significant figures, standard form — but it is the toolkit every other topic uses, so this page also carries the skills that are examined everywhere: choosing from the equation list, rearranging, proportion, EWAU, command words, graphs, and the practical-method questions.
howto: Start with the non-negotiables and do not move on from a section until its practice is green.
Read each explanation, then cover it and say it back. For a table of units or prefixes, test yourself with the flashcards at the bottom.
Study the worked example one step at a time and notice how the answer is laid out, not just what it is.
Do the practice questions before opening the hint or walkthrough. Calculations on paper in EWAU, then type the answer to check it.
For "explain" questions, write the answer in full sentences first, then compare it with the model answer point by point before you mark yourself.
Fill in the self-check at the end of each section. Anything red or amber is what to revise next.

bands.title: The non-negotiables
bands.blurb: Units, prefixes, conversions and the maths every calculation needs. These must be automatic: nothing in any other topic works without them.

bands.title: The tricky bits
bands.blurb: Working as a physicist: reading the question, command words, graphs, proportionality, planning and evaluating a practical, and estimating. These are the marks that are not about knowing any physics at all.

sections.title: SI units and the quantities they measure

parts.title: The units you must know
parts.html:
SI units are the standard set of units that all scientists use. The equations on the Edexcel sheet only work when every quantity is in its SI unit — that is why so much of physics is converting first.

temperaturekelvinKbase unit; °C is accepted where the question uses it
force, weightnewtonN$1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg m/s}^2$
energy, work donejouleJ$1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N m}$

Base units are the seven the system is built from (you meet six: m, kg, s, A, K and the mole). Every other unit is derived — built by multiplying or dividing base units, which is why $\text{m/s}$ is "metres divided by seconds".

parts.title: Capitals and symbols
parts.html:
A unit named after a person gets a capital symbol but a lower-case name: newton, N; joule, J; watt, W; hertz, Hz; pascal, Pa. Units not named after people are lower case: m, kg, s. Use the capital — it is the correct symbol, and examiners have only tolerated hz and c (June 2018 1H Q2: "accept hz"; June 2025 2H Q4: "allow c"). What loses the unit mark is a wrong unit: W s or W/s for watts (Nov 2021 1H Q8: "do NOT accept Ws, W/s"), N/m for a moment, kg/m/s for momentum. The exception to the capitals rule is the litre, L, which is capitalised to avoid confusion with 1.

Write compound units with a slash, as the exam papers do: $\text{m/s}$, $\text{kg/m}^3$, $\text{J/kg °C}$.

parts.title: Choosing the unit from the equation
parts.question: A student calculates $P = I \times V = 2 \times 12$. State the answer with its unit, and explain how the unit can be checked from the equation.
steps: $P = 2 \times 12 = 24$. Power is measured in watts, so $P = 24$ W.
Check from the equation: current in amps × potential difference in volts gives $\text{A} \times \text{V}$, and $1\ \text{A V} = 1\ \text{W}$. The unit of the answer follows from the units going in.
If the current had been in milliamps the answer would have come out in milliwatts — which is why everything is converted to SI units before substituting.

questions.text: What is the SI unit of mass?
questions.explain: The kilogram is the base unit of mass. Newtons measure weight (a force); grams and tonnes have to be converted.

questions.text: Which of these is a base unit?
questions.explain: The second is one of the base units. Newtons, joules and watts are derived from base units (a newton is a kg m/s²).

questions.text: A student writes an answer as "50 hz". What is wrong with it?
options: The symbol should be Hz, with a capital H
questions.explain: Hertz is named after Heinrich Hertz, so its symbol is Hz (capital H); the name stays lower case. Schemes have let hz through, but do not rely on it — and never change the unit itself (per second is s⁻¹ or Hz, never W/s).

questions.text: A rope is 2.5 km long. Give its length in the SI unit.
questions.hint: The SI unit of length is the metre; 1 km = 1000 m.

questions.text: A battery supplies a current of 45 mA. Give the current in the SI unit.
questions.hint: The SI unit of current is the ampere; 1 mA = 0.001 A.

questions.text: A student measures a pressure and writes the unit as N/m². Another student writes Pa. Explain why both are correct.
questions.model:
• Pressure = force ÷ area, so its unit is newtons per square metre, N/m².
  • The pascal is defined as 1 N/m² — it is the same unit with a special name.
  • Either is accepted; Pa is the SI name.

checklist: Give the SI unit for every quantity met at GCSE
Tell a base unit (m, kg, s, A, K, mol) from a derived unit (N, J, W …)
Write a unit with the correct symbol and capital letters (N not n, Hz not hz)
sections.blurb: Every quantity in physics has one standard unit. Exam answers need the right one every time: a number without a unit, or with the wrong one, loses the mark. A unit that matches your number scores even if it is not the SI one (2.68 g/cm³ earned all three marks in June 2023 2H Q3; 200 mC all three in June 2025 2H Q4) — the mark goes when the number is in one unit and the label says another (2680 g/cm³, 200 C).

parts.title: The seven prefixes
parts.html:

microμ$10^{-6}$ = 0.000 001a milliontha 50 μs pulse

Each step down the table from giga to kilo, and from milli to nano, is a factor of 1000. Centi is the odd one out (a factor of 100) and only really appears with metres.

Into the base unit: multiply by the prefix's value. $2.5\ \text{kW} = 2.5 \times 1000 = 2500$ W. Out of the base unit: divide. $0.004\ \text{A} = 0.004 \div 0.001 = 4$ mA.

parts.title: m means two things
parts.html: Lower-case m is both the metre and the prefix milli. Read $\text{mm}$ as "milli-metre" and $\text{ms}$ as "milli-second" — the prefix always comes first. And capital M (mega) is a million times bigger than small m (milli): $1\ \text{MW}$ is a million watts, $1\ \text{mW}$ is a thousandth of one.

parts.title: Stripping a prefix
parts.question: A laser emits light of wavelength 650 nm. Write the wavelength in metres.
steps: nano means $\times 10^{-9}$, so $650\ \text{nm} = 650 \times 10^{-9}$ m.
Keep it in standard form: it goes straight into $v = f \times \lambda$ without a counting-the-zeros mistake.

questions.text: What does the prefix mega mean?
questions.explain: Mega (M) means a million, 10⁶. Kilo is a thousand, giga a thousand million.

questions.text: A power station has an output of 2.5 MW. Give this in watts.
Which is the largest current?
questions.explain: Convert all to amps: $250 \muA = 0.000 25$ A; 25 mA = 0.025 A; 0.02 A; 2500 nA = 0.000 0025 A. 25 mA is largest.

questions.text: Write 500 nm in metres.
questions.hint: Nano = × 10⁻⁹.

questions.text: A kettle is labelled 3 kW. How many watts is that?
Explain the difference between 5 mW and 5 MW.
questions.model:
• m (milli) means a thousandth: 5 mW = 0.005 W.
  • M (mega) means a million: 5 MW = 5 000 000 W.
  • They differ by a factor of a thousand million (10⁹).

checklist: Recall what G, M, k, c, m, μ and n multiply by
Convert a value with a prefix into the base unit, and back again
Spot a prefix hidden in a question (a 2 kW kettle, a 250 nm wavelength)
sections.blurb: A prefix in front of a unit is a multiplier. Strip it off and apply the multiplier before any equation sees the number. Get it wrong and you lose one mark — the evaluation — and keep the rest: 3000 Hz instead of 30 000 Hz still scored 1 of 2 (June 2023 1H Q1(a)); sometimes the conversion is its own mark (June 2022 1H Q7(c)(i): "conversion of time to s (1)").

parts.title: km/h to m/s
parts.question: A car travels at 108 km/h. Convert this speed to m/s.
steps: Convert the distance: $108\ \text{km} = 108 \times 1000 = 108\,000$ m.
Convert the time: $1\ \text{h} = 60 \times 60 = 3600$ s.
Shortcut: $108 \div 3.6 = 30$ m/s. ✓

questions.text: A film lasts 90 minutes. How many seconds is that?
A tank holds 0.5 m³ of water. Give the volume in cm³.
A satellite takes 2.5 days to complete an orbit. Give this time in seconds.
questions.hint: Days → hours → seconds: × 24 × 3600.

questions.text: A cyclist's speed is 54 km/h. Convert this to m/s.
questions.hint: Divide by 3.6.

questions.text: An electric heater uses 1.5 kWh of energy. Give this in joules.
A student converts 20 cm² to m² and gets 0.2 m². What has gone wrong?
options: cm² cannot be converted to m²
questions.explain: 1 $m^2 = 100$ cm × 100 cm = 10 000 cm², so 20 cm² = $20 \div 10\,000 = 0.002$ m². Dividing by 100 only converts a length.

checklist: Convert minutes, hours and days into seconds
Convert km/h into m/s (and back)
Convert areas and volumes, remembering to square or cube the length conversion
Convert kWh into joules
sections.blurb: Minutes and hours into seconds, kilometres into metres, cubic centimetres into cubic metres. Convert first; the equation comes second.

sections.title: Significant figures and rounding

parts.title: Counting and rounding
parts.html:
Significant figures (s.f.) are the digits that carry information. Counting them:

  • All non-zero digits are significant: 3.52 has 3 s.f.
  • Zeros between non-zero digits are significant: 2.05 has 3 s.f.
  • Leading zeros are not: 0.0047 has 2 s.f. (the 4 and the 7).
  • Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant: 2.50 has 3 s.f. — it says the value is known to the hundredths.
  • Trailing zeros in a whole number are ambiguous: 1500 might be 2, 3 or 4 s.f. Standard form removes the doubt: $1.5 \times 10^3$ is 2 s.f.

Rounding to n s.f.: count n digits from the first non-zero digit; look at the next digit; 5 or more rounds up. Then keep the size of the number the same with zeros if needed: 48 367 to 2 s.f. is 48 000, not 48.

parts.title: How many to give
parts.html:
If the question says "to 2 significant figures", give exactly two. If it does not say, give the same number of significant figures as the least precise piece of data in the question — usually 2 or 3. If the question does not mention significant figures, the calculator value is accepted ("allow numbers that round to…", "ignore significant figures"). If it says "to 2 significant figures" or "to an appropriate number of significant figures", the rounding is a separate, independent mark: in June 2022 1H Q3(a)(iii) an answer of 1.4 (wrong value, right s.f.) scored 2 of 3 and 1.50 (right value, 3 s.f.) also scored 2 of 3. "Appropriate" means the same as the least precise data — 2 s.f. for 2 s.f. data.

Round only at the end. If you round part-way through a two-step calculation, the error grows. Keep the full calculator value (or at least one more figure than you will give) until the final line.

parts.title: Rounding a calculated answer
parts.question: A student calculates a density: $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V} = \dfrac{47}{18} = 2.611\,111\ldots$ g/cm³. The mass was measured to 2 s.f. and the volume to 2 s.f. Give the answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.
steps: The data has 2 significant figures, so the answer should too.
Count two digits from the first non-zero digit: 2.6|11… The next digit is 1, which is less than 5, so round down.
$\rho = 2.6$ g/cm³ (to 2 s.f.).
The answer line in the exam: \"2.6 g/cm³\". The full value stays in the working above it.

questions.text: How many significant figures does 0.0305 have?
questions.explain: Leading zeros do not count; the zero between the 3 and the 5 does. Three significant figures: 3, 0, 5.

questions.text: Round 0.047 83 to 2 significant figures.
questions.explain: The first significant figure is the 4. Two figures: 4, 7; the next digit (8) rounds the 7 up to 8: 0.048.

questions.text: Round 364 920 to 3 significant figures.
questions.explain: Three figures: 3, 6, 4; the next digit (9) rounds the 4 up to 5. Keep the size of the number with zeros: 365 000.

questions.text: A speed is calculated as 12.4873 m/s from a distance given to 2 s.f. and a time given to 3 s.f. How should the answer be given?
questions.explain: Match the least precise data: 2 significant figures. 12.4873 to 2 s.f. is 12 m/s.

questions.text: Which value is written to 3 significant figures?
questions.explain: 2.50 has three: the trailing zero after the decimal point is significant. 0.5 has one; 1500 is ambiguous; 3.1416 has five.

questions.text: A student finds a wave speed in two steps. She rounds the frequency to 1 s.f. after the first step, then uses it in the second. Explain why her final answer may be wrong, and what she should do instead.
questions.model:
• Rounding part-way through throws away information, so the error is carried into the second calculation and can grow.
  • She should keep the full (unrounded) value from the first step — or at least one extra figure — in the working.
  • Round only the final answer, to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data.

checklist: Count the significant figures in a number (including ones with leading zeros)
Round an answer to a stated number of significant figures
Choose a sensible number of significant figures when the question does not say
Keep full precision in the working and round only the final answer
sections.blurb: Give an answer to a sensible number of significant figures, round only at the end, and never give more figures than the data had.

sections.title: Standard form

parts.title: Reading and writing standard form
parts.html:
A number in standard form is written $a \times 10^{n}$, where $a$ is between 1 and 10 (it can be 1, but not 10) and $n$ is a whole number.

  • A positive power means a big number: $3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s is 300 000 000 m/s — the point moves 8 places to the right.
  • A negative power means a small number: $5 \times 10^{-7}$ m is 0.000 000 5 m — the point moves 7 places to the left.

Writing a number in standard form: move the decimal point until there is one non-zero digit in front of it; the number of places moved is $n$ (positive if the original number was 10 or more, negative if it was less than 1).

6 400 000$6.4 \times 10^{6}$6.4E6

On the calculator use the ×10ˣ key (sometimes marked EXP or EE): type 3.4, press ×10ˣ, type 8. Typing "3.4 × 10 ^ 8" also works but is where the brackets go wrong when you then divide by something.

parts.title: The E on the screen is not a unit
parts.html: A display of 2.5E-5 means $2.5 \times 10^{-5}$. Write it in the exam as $2.5 \times 10^{-5}$, never as "2.5E-5" or "2.5⁻⁵". And $12 \times 10^{4}$ is not standard form — the front number must be below 10: $1.2 \times 10^{5}$.

parts.title: A calculation with standard form
parts.question: Red light has a wavelength of $7 \times 10^{-7}$ m and travels at $3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s. Calculate its frequency using $v = f \times \lambda$.
steps: Rearrange: $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}$.
Enter on the calculator: 3 ×10ˣ 8 ÷ 7 ×10ˣ −7. The display shows 4.2857E14.
Sense check: the power is 8 − (−7) = 15 before the division by 7 brings it down to 14. Visible light is around $10^{14}$ Hz. ✓

questions.text: Write 300 000 000 in standard form. (Type it as 3e8.)
questions.hint: One non-zero digit in front of the point; count the places.

questions.text: Write 0.000 045 in standard form.
questions.hint: Small number, so the power is negative.
walkthrough: $0.000\,045 = 4.5 \times 10^{-5}$: the point moves 5 places to the right to get 4.5.

questions.text: Which of these is correctly written in standard form?
questions.explain: The number in front must be at least 1 and less than 10. Only 1.2 × 10⁴ qualifies.

questions.text: The radius of the Earth is $6.4 \times 10^{6}$ m. Give this in kilometres.
questions.hint: Divide by 1000, which lowers the power by 3.

questions.text: A calculator shows 1.6E-19 after a calculation. How should this be written on the answer line?
questions.explain: E on the display stands for × 10 to the power. Write the power of ten out in full.

questions.text: Which is the larger number: $2 \times 10^{-3}$ or $5 \times 10^{-4}$?
questions.explain: $2 \times 10^{-3} = 0.002$ and $5 \times 10^{-4} = 0.0005$. The less negative power wins, whatever the front number.

checklist: Write a large or small number in standard form
Convert from standard form to an ordinary number
Enter standard form on a calculator with the ×10ˣ (EXP) key, not by typing × 10 ^
Read a calculator display such as 3.2E-5 and write it correctly
sections.blurb: Very large and very small numbers written as a number between 1 and 10 times a power of ten. The calculator does the arithmetic; your job is to enter it correctly and read it back.

sections.title: The equation list: choosing the right equation

parts.title: The list, and how to use it
parts.html:
In the exam you are given a list of every equation in the course. You do not have to remember any of them. The skill the exam tests is selection: reading a question, listing the quantities it gives you and the one it wants, and finding the equation that contains exactly those.

  1. Write down the symbols for what is given: $m = \ldots$, $h = \ldots$, and the unknown with a question mark: $E = ?$
  2. Scan the list for an equation with those symbols and nothing else unknown. $g$ is normally printed in the question; if it is not, use $g = 10$ N/kg (the schemes also accept 9.8).
  3. If no equation has them all, it is a two-step question: find one that gets you a quantity the other needs (see the multi-step section).
  4. Copy the equation down exactly, symbols first — that is the E of EWAU.

Knowing the list well is still worth doing, because scanning thirty equations under time pressure is slow. Here it is, by topic:

In your own working, write what each symbol stands for the first time you use it: "$W$ = weight = …". It costs two seconds and stops you substituting a weight into a work equation.

parts.title: Picking the equation
parts.question: A question gives a mass of 2 kg, a height of 5 m and asks for the energy transferred when the object is lifted. Which equation, and why?
steps: List what is given: mass $m$, height $h$. Wanted: energy $E$.
Scan the list for an equation with $m$, $h$ and an energy: $\Delta GPE = m \times g \times \Delta h$. ($g = 10$ N/kg is a known constant, so it does not need to be given.)
Substitute: $GPE = 2 \times 10 \times 5 = 100$ J.
The method: list the given symbols, find the equation that contains exactly those and the unknown. It also tells you which quantity you have been given but do not need.

questions.text: A question gives a force and a distance moved in the direction of the force, and asks for the energy transferred. Which equation from the list?
questions.explain: Force, distance and an energy: work done, $E = F \times d$. Moment = $F \times d$ has the same symbols but gives a turning effect in N m, not an energy — read what the question asks for.

questions.text: In $W = m \times g$, what does $W$ stand for?
questions.explain: With mass and gravitational field strength, W is weight in newtons. Work done is $E = F \times d$.

questions.text: A question gives a current, a resistance and a time, and asks for the energy transferred. Which pair of equations do you need?
questions.explain: Current and resistance give power through $P = I^2R$; power and time give energy through $E = P \times t$. ($V = IR$ then $P = IV$ then $E = Pt$ also works — one step longer.)

questions.text: In $\Delta Q = m \times c \times \Delta\theta$, what is $Q$?
questions.explain: Here Q is thermal energy (J): mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change. The same letter means charge in $Q = I \times t$.

questions.text: A student is asked for the pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool and writes down $P = I \times V$. Explain the mistake and state the correct equation.
questions.model:
• $P = I \times V$ is electrical power; the symbol P means pressure in a different equation.
  • Pressure in a liquid: $P = h \times \rho \times g$ (depth × density × gravitational field strength).
  • The quantities given (depth, density) point to the right equation — match the symbols you have to the equation.

questions.text: A question gives an initial velocity, a final velocity and a distance, and asks for the acceleration. Which equation from the list?
questions.explain: No time is given, so the equation with u, v, a and x (and no t) is the one: $v^2 - u^2 = 2ax$. The first option needs a time you do not have.

questions.text: Describe how you would use the equation list to choose an equation for a calculation question.
questions.model:
• Write down the symbols for each quantity given in the question, and the symbol for the quantity asked for.
  • Scan the list for the equation that contains exactly those symbols ($g$ is usually printed; if not, use 10 N/kg).
  • If no single equation contains them all, find one that gives a quantity the other needs — a two-step calculation.
  • Copy the equation down exactly before substituting.

checklist: Know what is on the equation list, roughly where, so you can find an equation in seconds
Pick the right equation from the quantities a question gives you and the one it asks for
Recognise every symbol on the list, including the ones that mean two things
sections.blurb: Every equation is printed on a list in the exam. Nothing to memorise — but the list is no use unless you can find the one equation that fits the question, fast, and know what every symbol in it means.

sections.title: Rearranging an equation
equations: \text{Do the same thing to both sides}

parts.title: Two methods
parts.html:
Method 1 — the formula triangle works for any equation of the form one thing = two things multiplied, such as $F = m \times a$, $V = I \times R$, $v = f \times \lambda$, $\rho = m \div V$ (that is $m = \rho \times V$). Put the single quantity at the top; cover the one you want; what you can see is the answer.

Method 2 — do the same to both sides works for every equation, including the ones with squares and fractions that triangles cannot handle:

  1. Write the equation. Circle the quantity you want.
  2. Ask what is being done to it: multiplied by something? divided? squared? having something subtracted?
  3. Undo it, on both sides: divide to undo a multiply, multiply to undo a divide, square-root to undo a square, add to undo a subtract.
  4. Repeat until the quantity is on its own.
EquationMake … the subjectResultBecause
$KE = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$$v$$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times KE}{m}}$× 2, ÷ m, then square-root both sides
$a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$$v$$v = u + a t$× t to clear the fraction, then + u
$a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$$t$$t = \dfrac{v - u}{a}$× t, then ÷ a (t and a swap places)
$GPE = m g h$$h$$h = \dfrac{GPE}{m g}$÷ m and ÷ g
$P = \dfrac{E}{t}$$t$$t = \dfrac{E}{P}$× t, ÷ P

parts.title: Substitute first if the algebra scares you
parts.html: Marks are for the right answer with working, not for elegant algebra. If you cannot see how to rearrange $v^2 - u^2 = 2 a x$ for $a$, put the numbers in first: $0 - 20^2 = 2 \times a \times 50$, so $-400 = 100a$, so $a = -4$ m/s². Numbers are easier to push around than letters.

parts.title: Rearranging with a square
parts.question: A ball has 180 J of kinetic energy and a mass of 0.4 kg. Calculate its speed.
steps: Equation: $KE = \tfrac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2$. Wanted: $v$.
Undo the × ½ and the × m: $v^2 = \dfrac{2 \times KE}{m} = \dfrac{2 \times 180}{0.4} = 900$.
Undo the square with a square root: $v = \sqrt{900} = 30$ m/s.

Forgetting the square root (answering 900 m/s) is the most common lost mark on this equation — 900 m/s is nearly three times the speed of sound, which is the clue. It costs exactly one mark: in Nov 2020 2H Q6(c) the un-rooted value \"seen gains 2 marks\" of 3. The schemes also allow \"substitution and rearrangement in either order\", and June 2024 2H Q7(a) even credited substitution into a visibly wrong rearrangement — substituting first protects that mark.

questions.text: A resultant force of 1200 N acts on a car of mass 400 kg. Calculate the acceleration.
questions.hint: Cover a in the triangle: $a = F \div m$.

questions.text: A wave has speed 36 m/s and frequency 4 Hz. Calculate its wavelength using $v = f \times \lambda$.
questions.hint: $\lambda = v \div f$.

questions.text: An object gains 1500 J of gravitational potential energy when lifted 25 m. Calculate its mass. ($g = 10$ N/kg.)
questions.hint: $\text{GPE} = m g h$, so $m = \text{GPE} \div (g \times h)$.

questions.text: A 1600 kg car has 800 J of kinetic energy. Calculate its speed.
questions.hint: $v^2 = 2 \times \text{KE} \div m$, then square-root.

questions.text: A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 22.5 m/s in 5 s. Calculate its acceleration.
questions.hint: $a = (v - u) \div t$.

questions.text: A motor transfers 450 J of energy in 5 s. Calculate its power.
questions.hint: $P = E \div t$.

checklist: Make any quantity the subject of a three-term equation (triangle or algebra)
Rearrange an equation with a square (KE, spring energy) including the square root
Rearrange an equation with a fraction ($a = (v - u) \div t$) for the quantity on the top or the bottom
Substitute first, then rearrange, when the algebra looks hard
sections.blurb: The subject of an equation is the thing on its own. To make a different quantity the subject, undo what is being done to it, on both sides.

sections.title: Percentages, ratios and proportion

parts.title: Percentages and ratios
parts.html:
A percentage is a fraction with 100 on the bottom. Three jobs:

JobDo thisExample
Part as a percentage of a whole$\dfrac{\text{part}}{\text{whole}} \times 100$useful 30 J of 120 J in: $\dfrac{30}{120} \times 100 = 25\%$
A percentage of a quantity$\dfrac{\%}{100} \times \text{quantity}$40% of 500 J: $0.4 \times 500 = 200$ J
Percentage change$\dfrac{\text{new} - \text{old}}{\text{old}} \times 100$20 m/s to 25 m/s: $\dfrac{5}{20} \times 100 = 25\%$ increase

Divide by the original value, not the new one: 104 kPa → 74 kPa is −29%; dividing by 74 gives −41% and scored 1 of 2 (June 2024 2H Q4(c)(iii)). The change is 29%, not the 71% that remains (71% also scored 1 of 2). The sign is optional — the schemes write "(−) 29".

Efficiency is the percentage job in disguise: $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}}$, as a decimal or × 100 as a percentage. It can never be more than 1 (100%).

A ratio compares two quantities: a transformer with 200 turns on the primary and 50 on the secondary has a turns ratio of 4 : 1, so the voltage is divided by 4.

parts.title: Proportion
parts.html:
Directly proportional ($y \propto x$): double one, the other doubles; halve one, the other halves; the graph is a straight line through the origin. Force and extension of a spring (up to the limit), current and p.d. for a fixed resistor, distance and time at constant speed.

Inversely proportional ($y \propto \dfrac{1}{x}$): double one, the other halves. Pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature; acceleration and mass for a fixed force.

Proportional to the square ($y \propto x^2$): double one, the other goes up by $2^2 = 4$. Kinetic energy and speed; braking distance and speed.

The doubling test answers most "what happens if…" questions without a calculator. Look at the equation: if the quantity is on the top, the answer scales the same way; on the bottom, the opposite way; squared, by the square of the factor.

parts.title: A doubling question
parts.question: The kinetic energy of a car is 200 kJ. State the kinetic energy if its speed is trebled, and explain your answer.
steps: $KE = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$: kinetic energy is proportional to the square of the speed.
Trebling $v$ multiplies $v^2$ by $3^2 = 9$.
The sentence the examiner wants: \"KE is proportional to $v^2$, so trebling the speed makes the KE nine times bigger.\"

questions.text: A lamp transfers 200 J of energy, of which 60 J is useful light. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage.
questions.hint: Useful ÷ total × 100.

questions.text: A motor is 35% efficient. It is supplied with 2000 J. Calculate the useful energy output.
A car's speed increases from 20 m/s to 24 m/s. Calculate the percentage increase.
questions.hint: Change ÷ original × 100.

questions.text: The pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature is inversely proportional to its volume. The volume is halved. What happens to the pressure?
questions.explain: Inversely proportional: when one halves the other doubles.

questions.text: A spring extends by 3 cm with a 2 N load. The load is increased to 8 N. Calculate the new extension (Hooke's law applies).
questions.hint: Extension is directly proportional to force: the force is 4 times bigger.

questions.text: The braking distance of a car is proportional to the square of its speed. A driver doubles her speed. Explain what happens to the braking distance.
questions.model:
• Braking distance ∝ speed², so the distance scales with the square of the factor the speed changes by.
  • Doubling the speed multiplies speed² by 2² = 4.
  • The braking distance becomes four times as long.

checklist: Find a percentage of a quantity, and a quantity as a percentage of another
Calculate a percentage change
Use "directly proportional" and "inversely proportional" correctly in a sentence and in a calculation
Answer a "what happens if x is doubled" question without a calculator
sections.blurb: Efficiency, percentage change, scaling a recipe up: the same three skills behind a quarter of the marks on every paper.

sections.title: EWAU: how a calculation is marked

parts.title: Where the marks are
parts.html:
A 3-mark calculation is usually marked like this:

LineWhat you writeMark for
Equation$a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$choosing the right equation — usually marked together with the substitution ("selection and substitution (1)"); when the question prints the equation ("Use the equation …") there is no mark for copying it
Working$a = \dfrac{20 - 5}{6}$substituting the right numbers (a missed conversion usually keeps this mark and loses the evaluation mark instead)
Answer$= 2.5$evaluating correctly
Unitsm/s²only marked when the question says State the unit; then it is an independent mark (right unit with a wrong number still scores it). Otherwise the unit is printed for you on the answer line

Why it matters: a correct answer on its own gets full marks — "award full marks for the correct answer without working" is on almost every scheme (161 of the 177 Calculate parts in the past-paper bank). The working is insurance: with a slip on the calculator, the substitution line still earns 2 of the 3 marks; a wrong number on its own earns nothing. Two cases where working is compulsory: "Show that" (the given value alone "scores 0 marks", June 2022 1H Q5(a)(i)), and the separate unit or s.f. mark, which a bare number cannot earn.

Rearranging goes between E and W: write the equation as given, then the rearranged form, then substitute. Or substitute into the original and rearrange the numbers — both score.

Two-step questions get EWAU twice: finish the first quantity with its unit, then start the second equation on a new line.

parts.title: A full EWAU answer
parts.question: A kettle transfers 180 kJ of energy in 2 minutes. Calculate its power.
steps: Convert first: $180\ \text{kJ} = 180\,000$ J; $2\ \text{min} = 120$ s. (Conversions sit above the E line.)
E: $P = \dfrac{E}{t}$
U: W
Final answer line: $P = 1500$ W (or 1.5 kW). Every mark is visible on its own line.

questions.text: A student answers "calculate the weight of a 12 kg box" (2 marks) by writing only "12 N" and gets 0. A second student writes $W = m \times g = 12 \times 10 = 12$ N and gets 1. Explain the difference, and write the answer that earns both marks.
questions.model:
• The first student shows no substitution, so there is nothing to credit once the number is wrong; the second student's substitution line $12 \times 10$ earns the first mark even though the evaluation is wrong.
  • Full answer: $W = m \times g$; $W = 12 \times 10$; $= 120$; N.
  • A correct 120 N on its own would have scored both marks ("award full marks for the correct answer without working") — the working is what protects a slip.

questions.text: In a 3-mark calculation, which line usually earns the first mark?
options: The correct equation with the numbers substituted into it
questions.explain: The first mark is "selection and substitution" — the equation with the right numbers in it. The equation on its own scores only when the scheme lists "selection (1)" separately (June 2023 1H Q1(b), June 2025 1H Q8(a)(i)); the last mark is the evaluation.

questions.text: Write out, in EWAU layout, the calculation of the acceleration of a car that speeds up from 8 m/s to 20 m/s in 4 s.
questions.model:
• E: $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$
  • W: $a = \dfrac{20 - 8}{4} = \dfrac{12}{4}$
  • A: $= 3$
  • U: m/s²

questions.text: A question gives a time of 5 minutes. Where in an EWAU answer should the conversion to seconds appear?
options: Above the equation line, before substituting
questions.explain: Convert before you substitute: write 5 min = 300 s above the E line, so the W line uses 300.

checklist: Lay out every calculation as Equation, Working, Answer, Units
Show the substituted numbers, not just the equation and the answer
Earn the working marks even when the final answer is wrong
sections.blurb: Equation, Working, Answer, Units. Four lines, in that order, every time — because that is how the marks are given out.

sections.title: Key words: the definitions that score

parts.title: The definitions
parts.html:
Learn these as forms of words. In an evaluation, use the right word for the right idea — "the readings were precise but not accurate" is a mark; "the readings were good" is not.

TermDefinition that scoresCommon answer that does not
Independent variableThe variable you change (deliberately, in steps) — in an exam name the quantity ("thickness of aluminium", June 2024 1H Q8(d)(ii)), not "the one I change""the one on its own"
Dependent variableThe variable you measure (that changes as a result)"the one that depends" — on what?
Control variableA variable that is kept the same so that it does not affect the result"a variable you control" — say kept constant
ValidThe experiment tests what it claims to: only the independent variable is changed (a fair test)"correct"
AccurateClose to the true value"precise" / "correct"
PreciseRepeated readings are close to each other (little spread) — Edexcel has also marked "more precise" as readings to more significant figures / decimal places (June 2022 2H Q8(c)(ii))"accurate"
ResolutionThe smallest change in a quantity that an instrument can detect (or show)"how accurate the instrument is"
RepeatableThe same person, with the same method and equipment, gets the same result when the measurement is done again"you can repeat it"
ReproducibleA different person, or different method or equipment, gets the same result"you can do it again"
Random errorAn error that makes readings scatter unpredictably above and below the true value; reduced by repeating and averaging"human error"
Systematic errorAn error that shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction; not reduced by averaging"a big error"
Zero errorA systematic error where the instrument reads a non-zero value when it should read zero"an error of zero"
Anomalous resultA result that does not fit the pattern of the others; repeat it or leave it out of the mean"a wrong result"
UncertaintyThe range within which the true value is expected to lie; half the range of repeated readings"the error"
MeanThe sum of the readings divided by the number of readings, leaving out anomalies"the average" (accepted, but say how)
Directly proportionalDoubling one quantity doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin"a straight line" — it must go through the origin
Inversely proportionalDoubling one quantity halves the other; their product is constant"they go opposite ways"
Significant figuresThe digits in a value that carry meaning, counted from the first non-zero digit"the decimal places"

parts.title: The pairs that get swapped
parts.html: Accurate / precise: accurate is about the true value; precise is about the spread. Repeatable / reproducible: repeatable is the same person again; reproducible is someone else. Random / systematic: random scatters, systematic shifts. If you are writing one of these words, check you have not written its partner.

parts.title: Using the words in an evaluation
parts.question: A student measures the period of a pendulum five times with a stopwatch: 1.58, 1.62, 1.60, 1.59, 1.61 s. The accepted value is 1.80 s. Describe the quality of her results using the correct terms. (3)
steps: The readings are all within 0.04 s of each other: they are precise (small spread) and repeatable.
They are all about 0.2 s below the accepted value: they are not accurate.

Every reading is shifted the same way, so there is a systematic error — perhaps she timed from the wrong point of the swing, or the stopwatch was started late every time. Repeating more would not fix it.

parts.title: Key words

questions.text: State what is meant by a precise set of measurements. (1)
questions.model: • Measurements that are close to each other (little spread) when repeated.

questions.text: State what is meant by an accurate measurement. (1)
questions.model: • A measurement that is close to the true value.

questions.text: Which is the definition of resolution?
options: The smallest change in a quantity an instrument can detect
questions.explain: Resolution is the smallest change the instrument can show — 1 mm on a rule, 0.01 s on a stopwatch. It is not the same as accuracy.

questions.text: State the difference between a repeatable and a reproducible result. (2)
questions.model:
• Repeatable: the same person using the same method and equipment gets the same result again.
  • Reproducible: a different person, or a different method or equipment, gets the same result.

questions.text: A thermometer always reads 1 °C too high. This is:
questions.explain: Every reading is shifted by the same amount in the same direction: systematic (in fact a zero error). Averaging would not remove it.

questions.text: A student investigates how the extension of a spring depends on the force applied. Name the independent, dependent and one control variable. (3)
questions.model:
• Independent: the force applied (changed by adding masses).
  • Dependent: the extension (measured).
  • Control: the same spring (or the same original length / temperature) throughout.

questions.text: Which statement defines directly proportional?
options: The graph is a straight line
Doubling one quantity doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin
One quantity depends on the other
questions.explain: Proportional needs the straight line through the origin (or the constant ratio). A straight line with an intercept is linear, not proportional.

questions.text: State what is meant by a random error and give one way of reducing its effect. (2)
questions.model:
• An error that makes readings vary unpredictably (scatter) above and below the true value.
  • Reduce its effect by repeating the readings and calculating a mean.

parts.intro: Write each answer on paper first. Mark yourself strictly: if the bold words (or their equivalent) are missing, it is not a mark.

checklist: Define every bold term using the words the mark scheme credits
Tell accurate from precise, repeatable from reproducible, and random from systematic
Name the independent, dependent and control variables of any experiment
sections.blurb: The working-scientifically words are examined directly ("state what is meant by…") and indirectly (an evaluation that uses them correctly scores; one that uses them loosely does not).

sections.title: Command words: what the examiner wants

parts.title: The command words, and what scores
parts.html:
Command wordIt wantsModel one-liner
State / Give / Name / Write downA short answer, no reasoning. One word or one line."State the unit of power." — watt.
DescribeSay what happens or what something is like, in order. No why."Describe the motion shown." — It accelerates for 5 s, then moves at a constant 10 m/s.
ExplainSay why, with a reason or a mechanism. Use because, so, therefore."Explain why the car slows." — Friction acts backwards, so there is a resultant force opposite to the motion, so it decelerates.
CalculateA number, from an equation, with working and a unit (EWAU)."Calculate the speed." — $v = x \div t = 100 \div 8 = 12.5$ m/s.
DetermineA number, but you must get some of the data yourself — usually from a graph (a gradient, an area, a read-off)."Determine the acceleration from the graph." — draw the triangle, show the two values, divide.
Show thatThe answer is given; you must produce it with full working, to one more figure than quoted."Show that the force is about 50 N." — F = ma = $2.5 \times 20.4 = 51$ N ≈ 50 N.
EstimateA calculation with approximate data (the question gives "about …" values, or you read them off a graph); the answer is marked against a range. Show the read-off or the substitution: "reading off scale either 1750 or 1350 seen (1)" (June 2024 2H Q3(d))."Estimate how many gold atoms fit across 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m if one is 0.15 nm." — 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ ÷ 0.15 × 10⁻⁹ ≈ 2700 (June 2022 1H Q8(a): "any value that rounds to 2700").
CompareSimilarities and differences between both things named — mention both every time."Compare alpha and beta." — Both are ionising; alpha is more ionising but less penetrating. Similarities score too — "both straight lines (1)" in June 2022 2H Q4(c).
DiscussPoints for and against (or the evidence on each side), using the information given, then a conclusion that follows from them. Edexcel Physics says Discuss, not Evaluate — no 1PH0 paper 2018–2026 uses "Evaluate"."Discuss the arguments for and against using nuclear power…" (Nov 2020 1H Q8(c), 6 marks) — for … against … so overall …
Comment onDo the calculation the question points you to, then say whether the claim stands; the conclusion is an independent mark."Comment on this claim." — $t = 5.8$ h, so the claim is justified as the time is less than 6 hours (June 2023 2H Q8(b)(i)).
Use (the graph / data / Figure X)The answer must contain a value read from, or worked out from, the figure; quoting a number without doing anything with it does not score ("ignore simple quoting of data")."Use information from Figure 5." — doubling $V$ from 2 V to 4 V gives $R = 5.0$ Ω then $6.5$ Ω — not double.
DeviseA method question (see planning a practical); the stem tells you what must be in it ("how you will use your measurements")."Devise an experiment to…" — the seven steps.
DeduceCalculation → what it shows → conclusion, three marks in that order."Deduce how the resistors are arranged." — $R = 6 \div 1.2 = 5$ Ω; less than one 10 Ω resistor; so in parallel (June 2018 2H Q8(c)).
JustifyGive the evidence or reasoning for a statement that is given to you."Justify the teacher's claim that scattered count-rate readings are expected." — Radioactive decay is random, so the count rate is not constant and the readings vary. ("Difficult to predict" is refused: say random — Nov 2020 1H Q7(e)(ii).)
SuggestApply your knowledge to an unfamiliar situation; a sensible, physics-based idea scores even if it is not the one in the mark scheme."Suggest why the reading was lower." — some energy was transferred to the surroundings.
PredictSay what will happen, from the physics."Predict the current if the p.d. doubles." — it doubles (Ohm's law).
Draw / Sketch / PlotDraw: accurate with a ruler. Sketch: the shape and key features, labelled. Plot: points on given axes.
CompleteFill in the missing parts of a diagram, table or sentence.

The marks are in the word. A 2-mark "describe" is two things that happen; a 2-mark "explain" is one thing that happens and the reason for it.

parts.title: Describe is not explain
parts.html:
The most expensive habit at GCSE is answering every question with an explanation. "Describe how the velocity changes" is answered by reading the graph: it increases, then stays constant, then decreases to zero. Writing about forces there earns nothing, however correct. Likewise "explain" answered with a description — the ball slows down — scores nothing without the because.

Underline the command word before you read anything else.

parts.title: Same situation, three command words
parts.question: A ball is dropped and bounces. For each command word, write the kind of answer that scores: (a) Describe the motion of the ball as it falls. (b) Explain why the ball speeds up as it falls. (c) Calculate its speed after 2 s.
steps: (a) Describe: \"The ball starts from rest and its speed increases (it accelerates) all the way down.\" What happens — no reasons.
(b) Explain: \"The ball's weight acts downwards and there is no force balancing it, so there is a resultant force downwards, so the ball accelerates (Newton's second law).\" Each so is a reason.
(c) Calculate: $v = u + a t = 0 + 10 \times 2 = 20$ m/s. Equation, working, answer, unit.
Three questions about one ball; three different answers. The command word decides which.

questions.text: "Describe how the current changes as the potential difference is increased." Which answer scores?
options: The current increases because the electrons are pushed harder
questions.explain: Describe wants what happens, not why. The first option is an explanation — correct physics, wrong command word.

questions.text: "Explain why a parachutist reaches a terminal velocity." Which answer scores full marks?
options: Air resistance increases with speed until it equals the weight, so the resultant force is zero, so the velocity stays constant
Terminal velocity is the maximum velocity
questions.explain: Explain needs the chain of reasons: air resistance grows → balances weight → zero resultant → constant velocity. The others describe or give half a reason.

questions.text: What does "determine" usually mean in a graph question?
options: Read or work out a value from the graph, showing how
questions.explain: Determine means find a value, and you must get some of the data from the graph yourself — a gradient triangle, an area or a read-off, shown on the graph.

questions.text: A question says: "Show that the kinetic energy of a 1250 kg car moving at 15 m/s is about 140 kJ." Write the answer that earns full marks.
questions.model:
• $KE = \tfrac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2$
  • $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1250 \times 15^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1250 \times 225$ — every number must be seen in the substitution ("all three numbers needed to show that").
  • $= 140\,625$ J $= 141$ kJ ≈ 140 kJ. Write the unrounded value: the quoted number on its own "scores 0 marks" (June 2022 1H Q5(a)(i)), and in June 2024 1H Q7(a)(ii) "712 or 713 m" scored where the quoted "710 m" did not.

questions.text: "Compare the properties of alpha and beta radiation." A student writes: "Alpha is stopped by paper and is very ionising." Explain why this answer scores poorly, and improve it.
questions.model:
• A compare answer must mention both things in the question — this answer only talks about alpha.
  • It should pair each property: alpha is stopped by paper whereas beta passes through paper and is stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
  • Alpha is more ionising than beta. Both are ionising (a similarity) — one similarity and two differences is a safe shape.

questions.text: A 6-mark "discuss the arguments for and against…" question. What must the answer contain to reach the top band?
options: A list of facts about the topic
Points for and against, using the data given, and a conclusion that follows from them
questions.explain: Discuss = weigh up. Both sides, drawing on the information in the question, then a judgement that is justified by the points made. (Edexcel Physics writes Discuss; no 1PH0 paper has used Evaluate.)

checklist: Tell a describe question from an explain question, and answer each the right way
Know what calculate, determine and show that each require
Structure an evaluate or compare answer so both sides and a conclusion appear
sections.blurb: The first word of a question tells you what kind of answer scores. Answer a "describe" with an explanation and you have wasted the marks on the wrong thing.

sections.title: Reading the question

parts.title: A routine for every calculation question
parts.html:
1. Underline the command word and read the last sentence first: it says what to find and how to give it ("to 2 s.f.", "in kJ", "include the sign").
  2. List every value as symbol = number unit. $m = 250$ g, $t = 3$ min, $v = 15$ m/s. Write the unknown with a question mark: $P = ?$
  3. Convert anything not in SI: 250 g → 0.25 kg; 3 min → 180 s; 2 kW → 2000 W. Cross out the old value so you cannot pick it up by mistake.
  4. Check the stem for the constants: the speed of light is always printed, $g$ usually is ($g = 10$ N/kg, or 9.8 — both accepted). The values that are not given are the hidden ones: $u = 0$ for "from rest", the halving of distance or time for an echo. (Speed of sound, density of water and specific heat capacity of water are given.)
  5. Cross out distractors: a question that gives a car's mass, speed and colour of paint — or its mass, speed and the length of the road — may include a value you do not need. If a symbol does not appear in your equation, leave it.
  6. Look back at the earlier parts: part (c) often needs the answer to part (b). "Use your answer to (b)" means exactly that, even if (b) was wrong — the marks follow through.

parts.title: The traps, named
parts.html:
TrapWhat it looks likeDefence
Mixed units"a 500 g mass … 2 km … 5 minutes"Convert in the list, before any equation
Diameter for radius, or area given as a length"a pipe of diameter 4 cm" then a question needing the radius or the areaRead the quantity's name, not just its number
Weight for mass"a 600 N box" used in $F = m a$A value in newtons is a weight; divide by $g$ to get the mass
Total vs per second"transfers 3000 J every minute" in a power questionPower is per second: ÷ 60
Stated precision"Give your answer to 2 significant figures"Circle it; round at the end
Hidden zero"starts from rest", "comes to a stop", "dropped", "at the top of its flight"$u = 0$ or $v = 0$
Opposite directions"in the opposite direction", "rebounds", "thrown upwards"One velocity (or momentum) is negative: the change is $0.80 - (-0.60) = 1.4$, not $0.2$ (June 2023 1H Q9(b), where 0.2 lost the evaluation mark). The sign on the final answer itself is optional — schemes write "(−)150 N"

parts.title: A question with three traps
parts.question: A cyclist of mass 70 kg, riding a 12 kg bicycle, travels 540 m along a flat road in 3 minutes. Calculate the cyclist's average speed in m/s.
steps: Last sentence first: average speed, in m/s. So the answer needs metres and seconds.
List: $m_\text{cyclist} = 70$ kg, $m_\text{bike} = 12$ kg, $x = 540$ m, $t = 3$ min. Wanted: $v = ?$
Convert: $3\ \text{min} = 180$ s. Distractors: the two masses — speed does not depend on them. Cross them out.
A sense check costs five seconds: 3 m/s is a gentle cycling speed. ✓

questions.text: A bag of sugar has a mass of 250 g. Calculate its weight. ($g = 10$ N/kg.)
questions.hint: Grams to kilograms first.

questions.text: A lift raises a 300 kg load through 2.5 km of mine shaft in 5 minutes. Calculate the average speed of the lift in m/s.
questions.hint: Which values does speed need? Convert those; ignore the rest.
walkthrough: $2.5\ \text{km} = 2500$ m; $5\ \text{min} = 300$ s. The mass is not needed.

questions.text: A 800 g ball is thrown at 12 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
questions.hint: 800 g = 0.8 kg; square the speed.

questions.text: A heater transfers 400 J of energy every second. It is 75% efficient. Calculate the useful power output.
questions.hint: 400 J every second is a power of 400 W. Then take 75% of it.

questions.text: A question says: "A stone is dropped from a bridge. Calculate its speed after falling for 1.5 s." Which value is given without being written down?
options: The initial speed, $u = 0$, because it is dropped
questions.explain: "Dropped" means it starts from rest: $u = 0$. With $a = g = 10$ m/s², $v = 0 + 10 \times 1.5 = 15$ m/s. No height or mass is needed.

questions.text: A ball hits a wall with momentum 0.80 kg m/s and rebounds with momentum 0.60 kg m/s in the opposite direction; the contact lasts 0.070 s. A student writes $\Delta p = 0.80 - 0.60 = 0.20$ kg m/s and $F = 2.9$ N, and gets 2 marks of 3. Explain the mistake and give the full answer.
questions.model:
• The ball reverses, so the final momentum is $-0.60$ kg m/s: $\Delta p = 0.80 - (-0.60) = 1.4$ kg m/s.
  • $F = \Delta p \div t = 1.4 \div 0.070 = 20$ N (June 2023 1H Q9(b): "answers which round to (±) 2.9 scores 2 marks" — the direction slip costs the evaluation mark only).
  • Reading "in the opposite direction" as a minus sign before writing anything would have caught it.

checklist: Pull out every value with its unit, and convert the ones that need it, before starting
Spot the quantities given that are not needed, and the standard values not given
Notice instructions such as "to 2 significant figures", "ignore air resistance", "include the sign"
Use information from earlier parts of a question in later parts
sections.blurb: Most lost marks are not physics mistakes. They are a number in the wrong unit, a value that was given but not needed, or an instruction in the last line that was never read.

sections.title: Multi-step calculations

parts.title: Finding the chain
parts.html:
A 4- or 5-mark calculation almost always needs two equations. The method:

  1. Write the equation that contains the quantity you want. Which of its inputs are you missing?
  2. Find an equation that gives that missing quantity from the values you do have. That is step one.
  3. Do step one in full, with its unit. Do step two with the unrounded result.

Chains that come up again and again:

WantGivenChain
force on a carmass, change in speed, time$a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$ then $F = m a$
energy from the mainscurrent, p.d., time$P = I V$ then $E = P t$
work done liftingmass, height$W = m g$ then $E = F \times d$ (or $GPE = m g h$ in one go)
mass of a blockdimensions, density$V = l \times w \times h$ then $m = \rho V$
speed at the bottom of a dropheight$GPE = m g h$, set $KE = GPE$, then $v = \sqrt{2 KE / m}$
power of a motorforce, distance, time$E = F d$ then $P = E / t$
wavelengthspeed, period$f = 1 / T$ then $\lambda = v / f$

parts.title: Do not round in the middle
parts.html: If step one gives $a = 2.666\,6\ldots$ m/s², use 2.6666 (or the calculator's memory) in step two, not 2.7. Rounding to 2.7 then multiplying by 1500 kg gives 4050 N instead of 4000 N. The scheme usually forgives this ("accept 2, 2.2, 2.27, 2.3 for a throughout", June 2022 1H Q5(a)(ii)) but not always (Nov 2020 1H Q5(a) gave 1 mark, not 2, for a final 1.5 m reached through a rounded wavelength) — carrying the full value is the only way to be sure.

parts.title: Two equations, one chain
parts.question: A car of mass 1500 kg accelerates from rest to 24 m/s in 8 s. Calculate the resultant force on the car.
steps: Want: force. $F = m \times a$ — have $m$, missing $a$.
Get $a$ from the speeds and time: $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{24 - 0}{8} = 3$ m/s².
Now $F = m \times a = 1500 \times 3 = 4500$ N.
Two EWAUs, each with its unit; the second uses the first's unrounded result.

questions.text: A 1200 kg car travels 60 m in 3 s at constant speed.

parts.hint: $p = m \times v$ with the speed from (a).
parts.label: b

questions.text: A 230 V hairdryer draws a current of 2.5 A for 3 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.
questions.hint: Power first ($P = IV$), then energy ($E = P t$) with the time in seconds.

questions.text: A crane lifts a 50 kg load through 12 m. Calculate the work done. ($g = 10$ N/kg.)
questions.hint: Weight first, then work = force × distance.

questions.text: A steel block measures 2 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm. The density of steel is 8000 kg/m³. Calculate the mass of the block.
questions.hint: Volume in m³ first (convert each length to metres), then $m = \rho \times V$.

questions.text: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from a height of 1.8 m. Ignore air resistance. ($g = 10$ N/kg.)

parts.text: Calculate the gravitational potential energy lost by the ball as it falls.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the speed of the ball just before it hits the ground.
parts.hint: All the GPE becomes KE: ½ $m v^2 = 9$ J, then square-root.
parts.label: b

questions.text: A student calculates a force in two steps. In step one she gets an acceleration of 1.333… m/s² and writes it down as 1 m/s². In step two she multiplies by 900 kg and gets 900 N; the mark scheme says "allow numbers that round to 1200". Explain why she lost the final mark and what she should have done.
questions.model:
• She rounded the intermediate value (1.333… to 1) and the rounding error was multiplied up in step two.
  • 1.333… × 900 = 1200 N; $1 \times 900 = 900$ N, which does not round to 1200. (A gentler rounding — 1.3 → 1170 N — is usually forgiven, but not always.)
  • Carry the full value (or at least one extra significant figure) between steps; round only the final answer.

checklist: Plan the chain: which equation gives the quantity the second equation needs?
Carry the full value from step one into step two
Lay out each step as its own EWAU with its own unit
Check that the final unit matches what was asked for
sections.blurb: Two equations, one after the other. The hard part is seeing which quantity links them, and not rounding in between.

sections.title: Graph skills: plotting, best fit, gradient

parts.title: Plotting and the line of best fit
parts.html:
Axes: the independent variable (the one you changed) goes on the $x$-axis, the dependent (the one you measured) on the $y$-axis. Label each with quantity in unit, as Edexcel does: extension in m. Scale: pick a scale so the points fill more than half the grid in each direction, going up in 1s, 2s, 5s or 10s (never 3s or 7s). The axes do not have to start at zero — unless you need the origin, for proportionality or an intercept.

Points: small, neat crosses (×). Aim for half a small square; the schemes allow ±1 small square (June 2022 2H Q4(b)(i): "points plotted to within ± 1 small square"), and a cross whose centre cannot be found is one that cannot be checked.

Line of best fit: a single thin straight line (ruler) or smooth curve that follows the trend with about as many points above it as below. It does not join the dots, does not have to pass through every point, and does not have to go through the origin unless the physics says so. An anomalous point — one clearly off the trend — is circled and ignored. Draw the line once: a second attempt alongside the first ("tramlining") loses the mark, while a slightly shaky single line does not (June 2022 2H Q4(b)(ii)); the examiner judges it by eye against a band on the scheme. If asked why a gradient from scattered points is only an estimate: the points are scattered about the line, so many lines of best fit — and gradients — are possible (Nov 2021 1H Q4(d)(iii)).

parts.title: Gradient and intercept
parts.html:
To find a gradient:

  1. Draw a right-angled triangle on the line of best fit, as large as possible — at least half the length of the line. The method mark is for "two points on the line" or "attempt at Δy/Δx"; the value must then land inside the tolerance (3.90 ± 0.10 N/m in June 2025 1H Q2(b)(iii)), which a small triangle often misses.
  2. For a curve, "determine the gradient at …" means draw a tangent at that point first — the tangent is the first mark and the value mark depends on it (June 2025 1H Q6(b)(ii): "tangent drawn to curve (1) … dependent on MP1"). Then take the gradient of the tangent with a large triangle.
  3. Use two points on the line where it crosses grid lines, not two of the plotted data points (they are not on the line).
  4. $\text{gradient} = \dfrac{\text{change in } y}{\text{change in } x}$, with the two values read from the axes and written down.
  5. The gradient has a unit: $y$-unit per $x$-unit. For force against extension it is N/m — the spring constant.

The intercept is where the line crosses the $y$-axis (at $x = 0$). It usually means a value "at the start" or a fixed offset: the initial velocity on a $v$–$t$ graph, the friction that must be overcome before a trolley moves, the resistance of the leads in a circuit.

graph.alt: Force against extension: six plotted points scattered closely around a straight line of best fit from the origin to (0.12, 3.0).

parts.after: In the graph above, the triangle from A to B spans most of the line: $\text{gradient} = \dfrac{3.0 - 1.0}{0.12 - 0.04} = \dfrac{2.0}{0.08} = 25$ N/m. Using two data points instead (say the first and last) would give 23.0 N/m — close, but it is not what the line says, and the examiner is checking that you used the line.

parts.title: Determining a value from a graph
parts.question: The graph in the explanation shows force against extension for a spring. Determine the spring constant.
steps: The spring constant is the gradient of a force–extension graph ($F = k \times x$, so $k = F \div x$).
Choose two points on the line of best fit on gridline crossings: A $(0.04,\ 1.0)$ and B $(0.12,\ 3.0)$.
$k = 25$ N/m. The unit comes from the axes: newtons on $y$ per metre on $x$.

questions.text: The graph shows the velocity of a car.

parts.text: Determine the gradient of the line.
parts.hint: Pick two points on the line: (0, 4) and P (10, 24).

parts.text: State the intercept on the velocity axis.
parts.hint: Where the line meets the vertical axis.

graph.alt: Velocity–time graph: a straight line from (0, 4) to (10, 24).

parts.text: Determine the gradient of the line of best fit.
parts.hint: Use the line, not the points: it runs from the origin to (1.0, 5.0).
parts.label: a

parts.text: Why is a large triangle used to find the gradient?
options: Reading errors on the axes are a smaller fraction of a large change, so the gradient is more accurate
The line is only straight in the middle

parts.label: b

parts.text: The point at 0.6 m lies slightly above the line. Explain whether the student should have drawn the line through it.
parts.model:
• No. A line of best fit follows the overall trend of all the points, with points balanced on either side.
  • It does not need to pass through every point (or any of them); the scatter is normal experimental variation.
  • Only a point far from the trend is treated as anomalous — this one is close to the line and is simply left where it is.
parts.label: c

questions.text: A walker covers 20 m in the first 4 s, stands still for 2 s, then walks a further 20 m in the next 2 s. Draw the distance–time graph on the grid (tap the grid to place the points in order, or draw it on paper).

grid.alt: A blank grid for drawing on

answerGraph.alt: Distance–time graph: 0 to 20 m in 4 s, flat to 6 s, then 20 m to 40 m by 8 s.
