questions.text: A student's $y$-axis scale goes up in 3s (0, 3, 6, 9 …). Why would this lose a mark?
options: Points cannot be plotted accurately when each small square is an awkward fraction
It would not lose a mark
questions.explain: With 3 per large square each small square is 0.3 — hard to plot and to read. Scales go up in 1, 2, 5 or 10 (× any power of ten).

checklist: Choose axes and a scale that use more than half the grid, with sensible intervals
Plot points as small crosses, accurate to half a small square
Draw a line (or smooth curve) of best fit with roughly equal points either side, ignoring anomalies
Find a gradient from a triangle that spans at least half the line, using points on the line, not data points
Read an intercept and say what it means
sections.blurb: Plotting with the right scale, drawing a line of best fit through the scatter, and taking a gradient from a big triangle. Each is a mark, and each is lost the same way every year.

sections.title: Proportionality: from graphs and from data

parts.title: Proportional, linear, or neither
parts.html:
RelationshipGraphTest with numbersSay
Directly proportional, $y \propto x$Straight line through the origin$y \div x$ is the same for every pair"$y$ is directly proportional to $x$"
Linear with an interceptStraight line not through the originequal steps in $x$ give equal steps in $y$, but $y \div x$ changes"$y$ increases linearly with $x$" — not proportional
Inversely proportional, $y \propto \dfrac{1}{x}$Curve falling towards the axis, never touching it$x \times y$ is the same for every pair"As $x$ increases, $y$ decreases, and the graph is non-linear" — claim inverse proportion only after checking that $x \times y$ is constant; from the shape alone the examiners have both allowed it (June 2022 2H Q8) and ignored it (June 2025 2H Q7)
Proportional to the square, $y \propto x^2$Curve getting steeper through the origin$y \div x^2$ is constant; doubling $x$ gives $4y$"$y$ is proportional to $x$ squared"

graph.alt: Two parallel straight lines: A from the origin to (10, 20), B from (0, 5) to (10, 25). Only A shows direct proportion.

parts.after: Line A passes through the origin: doubling $x$ from 4 to 8 doubles $y$ from 8 to 16 — proportional. Line B has the same gradient but an intercept of 5: doubling $x$ from 4 to 8 takes $y$ from 13 to 21, not double. B is linear, and "$y$ increases by the same amount for each unit increase in $x$" is the correct description; "proportional" would be marked wrong.

parts.title: Inverse proportion looks like this
parts.html:
Pressure against volume for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature ($P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$). Every point on the curve has $P \times V = 20$: $(1, 20)$, $(2, 10)$, $(4, 5)$, $(8, 2.5)$. The curve never reaches either axis.

To get a straight line from an inverse relationship, plot $y$ against $\dfrac{1}{x}$ — then it goes through the origin like any proportional graph.

graph.alt: A curve falling from (1, 20) towards the x-axis: pressure against volume at constant temperature.

parts.title: Testing a data table
parts.question: A student records the current through a component at several potential differences: 2 V → 0.4 A; 4 V → 0.8 A; 6 V → 1.2 A; 8 V → 1.5 A. Is the current directly proportional to the potential difference?
steps: The ratio is constant for the first three pairs and drops for the last, so the current is proportional to the p.d. up to about 6 V, then increases less than proportionally.
On a graph this is a straight line through the origin that starts to curve over — the resistance is increasing (a filament lamp getting hot).

The sentence: \"Up to 6 V, $I$ is directly proportional to $V$ because $I \div V$ is constant (0.2 A/V) — doubling $V$ from 2 V to 4 V doubles $I$ from 0.4 A to 0.8 A; above 6 V it is not, because the ratio falls.\" Show the division or the doubling: copying the numbers out of the table \"scores nothing for this mark\" (June 2019 2H Q3(b)(ii): \"ignore simple quoting of data\"). To test for proportion by experiment: more values over a bigger range, then $y \div x$ for each pair — \"if the ratio is the same they are proportional\" (Nov 2021 2H Q6(c)) — or a straight line through the origin.

questions.text: A graph of extension against force is a straight line through the origin up to 8 N, then curves upwards. Which statement is correct?
options: Extension is proportional to force for all forces shown
Extension is proportional to force up to 8 N only
Extension is never proportional to force
Extension is inversely proportional to force
questions.explain: Through the origin and straight = proportional. Where the line curves, equal increases in force no longer give equal increases in extension — the limit of proportionality has been passed.

questions.text: The kinetic energy of an object is 4 J at a certain speed. Calculate the kinetic energy when the speed is doubled.
questions.hint: $\text{KE} \propto v^2$: double v, multiply KE by 2² = 4.

questions.text: A gas has a pressure of 12 kPa at a volume of 2 m³. The temperature stays the same and the volume is increased to 6 m³. Calculate the new pressure.
questions.hint: Inversely proportional: $P \times V$ is constant.

questions.text: A set of results: $x = 2$, $y = 7$; $x = 4$, $y = 11$; $x = 6$, $y = 15$. Which description is correct?
options: y is directly proportional to x
y increases linearly with x but is not proportional to it
y is inversely proportional to x
questions.explain: Equal steps (x up by 2, y up by 4) make it linear, but $y \div x$ is 3.5, 2.75, 2.5 — not constant — so it is not proportional. The line would have an intercept of 3.

questions.text: Describe the graph you would expect if you plotted the current through a fixed resistor against the potential difference across it, and state what the graph shows about the relationship.
questions.model:
• A straight line through the origin.
  • This shows the current is directly proportional to the potential difference (Ohm's law), because doubling V doubles I.
  • The gradient is $1 \div R$ (or: the resistance is constant).

questions.text: A student plots pressure against volume for a gas and gets a curve. Explain how she could plot the data to get a straight line, and what the line would show.
questions.model:
• Plot pressure against 1 ÷ volume (or volume against 1 ÷ pressure).
  • If pressure is inversely proportional to volume this gives a straight line through the origin.
  • Because $P \propto 1/V$ means $P \times V$ is constant: the gradient of the line is that constant.

checklist: State what a graph must show for two quantities to be directly proportional
Test a data table for direct proportion (constant $y \div x$) and inverse proportion (constant $x \times y$)
Describe a straight-line graph with an intercept correctly (linear, not proportional)
Use a proportionality to predict a value
sections.blurb: "Directly proportional" is a precise claim: a straight line through the origin, or a constant ratio. A straight line on its own is not enough.

sections.title: Planning a practical: the 6-mark method question

parts.title: Seven steps, every time
parts.html:
Whenever a question says describe how you would investigate, plan an experiment or design a method, write your answer in these seven steps, in this order. A 6-mark method question is levelled: the examiner has a list of indicative content — the equipment and what each piece measures, what is changed and what is kept the same, how the results are processed — and awards Level 1, 2 or 3 for how much of it your answer covers in a logical order. The seven steps make sure every item on that list is there. (A 3- or 4-mark version is point-marked, "any four from" a similar list.)

  1. Read the question, and write down the two variables you are being asked to investigate. One is the thing you will change (the independent variable); the other is the thing you will measure (the dependent variable).
  2. Figure out which formula links them. Write it down. It tells you what else must be kept the same, and what to do with the results at the end.
  3. Say which one you will change and how you will change it — e.g. "add masses to the trolley". Give a range or a number of values ("five different masses"), and say what you will keep the same so it is a fair test.
  4. Say which one you will measure, and how you will measure it, including the equipment to use — e.g. "record the speed at each light gate, and measure the distance between them with a ruler".
  5. Say what you will do with the result — e.g. "use $a = F \div m$ to calculate the acceleration" or "plot a graph of $F$ against $a$ and calculate the gradient".
  6. Add a detail about the practical to make sure you get accurate results — e.g. "release the trolley from the same point each time", "keep the ramp at the same angle", "use light gates rather than a stopwatch so there is no reaction time". One specific, relevant detail is enough.
  7. Say you will repeat the readings and calculate a mean. Write both halves as one phrase: where a scheme credits repeats it usually credits the pair as one point ("repeat and average time (1)", June 2023 1H Q2(b)(i)), and has only sometimes credited "repeat" alone. In a 6-mark levelled answer it is one line of indicative content among many. And in a question that asks how to make the result more accurate or to improve the procedure, repeating is ignored (six schemes 2018–2023, e.g. June 2019 2H Q7(a): "ignore reference to repeating and taking average") — give a change to the method instead.

Write the steps as numbered points, not as one paragraph. Draw the apparatus and label it — the schemes say "marks may be scored from the diagram" and "credit all elements seen in diagram or stated" (June 2024 2H Q7(b)(i), Q9(d)). For a circuit it is essential: ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the component, variable resistor in series to change the pd or keep the current small (June 2018 2H Q10(b) indicative content starts "Circuit diagram including…").

parts.title: Where the marks go missing
parts.html: The two most common ways to lose marks are describing the equipment without saying what you measure with it ("use a voltmeter" earns nothing; "use a voltmeter to measure the potential difference across the wire" does), and stopping after you have collected the data. The question asked how you would investigate the link between the two variables, so the calculation or graph that shows the link is a mark in its own right. And write "repeat and calculate a mean" as one phrase — "repeat" by itself has sometimes scored and sometimes not.

parts.title: Investigating resistance and length
parts.question: Describe how you would investigate how the resistance of a wire depends on its length. (6 marks)
steps: Step 1 — the two variables. I am investigating length of wire (independent, the one I change) and resistance (dependent, the one I measure).
Step 2 — the formula. Resistance is found from $R = V \div I$, so I need to measure the potential difference across the wire and the current through it. I expect $R$ to be proportional to length.

Step 3 — what I change and how. Stretch the wire along a metre rule and connect it into a circuit with crocodile clips. Change the length by moving one clip along the wire: 20 cm, 40 cm, 60 cm, 80 cm, 100 cm. Keep the same wire and the same cell, and use a variable resistor in series to keep the current small, because current heats the wire and raises its resistance (June 2023 2H Q2(b)(iv)).

Step 4 — what I measure and how. For each length, read the potential difference across the wire with a voltmeter in parallel, and the current with an ammeter in series. Measure the length with the metre rule.
Step 5 — what I do with the results. Calculate $R = V \div I$ for each length, then plot a graph of resistance against length. A straight line through the origin shows $R \propto$ length.
Step 6 — accuracy. Switch the circuit off between readings so the wire does not warm up (its resistance would rise), and check the ammeter reads zero with the circuit open.
Step 7 — repeat and mean. Take three readings of $V$ and $I$ at each length and calculate a mean resistance before plotting.

As it would be written in the exam: seven numbered sentences, one per step — about ten lines. Every sentence contains either a variable, a piece of equipment and what it measures, or what is done with a number.

parts.title: Planning a practical

questions.text: A student has a spring, a clamp stand, a metre rule and a set of 100 g masses. Describe how the student could investigate how the extension of the spring depends on the force applied to it. (6 marks)
questions.model:
6 marks — one mark per row below, any 6 of the 7.

PointForWhat you need to write
1VariablesIdentifies the two variables: the force (weight of the hanging masses) is changed (independent) and the extension is measured (dependent).
2FormulaStates that they are linked by $F = k \times x$ (Hooke's law), with $F = m \times g$ giving the force from each mass.
3ChangeChanges the force by adding 100 g masses one at a time (at least five values), using the same spring throughout.
4MeasureMeasures the extension with the metre rule: reads the original length, reads the new length and subtracts (both readings named — Nov 2020 2H Q6(a)(ii)), at eye level against a pointer.
5Use the resultPlots a graph of force against extension; a straight line through the origin shows $F \propto x$ and the gradient is the spring constant $k$.
6AccuracyOne specific detail: reads the rule at eye level to avoid parallax, or fixes a pointer to the spring, or does not exceed the limit of proportionality (checks the spring returns to its original length); or uses a rule with millimetre divisions held close to the spring, or adds the masses in smaller steps / over a larger range (Nov 2020 2H Q6(a)(iii)).
7Repeat & meanRepeats the readings for each force (e.g. by unloading and reloading) and calculates a mean extension — write both halves as one phrase.
  • "Use a ruler" on its own does not earn the Measure mark — say what is measured and how the extension is found from it.
  • The Use the result mark needs the graph (or the calculation of $k$), not just "record the results in a table".
questions.hint: Step 1: the variables are force and extension. What do you add to change the force, and what must you subtract to get the extension?

questions.text: Describe how you would investigate how the current through a filament lamp depends on the potential difference across it. (6 marks)
questions.model:
6 marks — one mark per row below, any 6 of the 7.

PointForWhat you need to write
1VariablesIdentifies the two variables: the potential difference across the lamp is changed (independent) and the current through it is measured (dependent).
2FormulaStates that they are linked by $V = I \times R$, and that for a filament lamp the resistance is expected to increase as it heats up.
3ChangeChanges the potential difference using a variable resistor (or a variable power supply) in series, taking at least five values from zero upwards, using the same lamp.
4MeasureMeasures the current with an ammeter in series with the lamp and the potential difference with a voltmeter in parallel across it.
5Use the resultPlots a graph of current against potential difference (an $I$–$V$ graph); a curve that flattens shows the resistance increasing. Or calculates $R = V \div I$ at each p.d. and shows it rising.
6AccuracyOne specific detail: switches off between readings so the lamp cools between measurements, or reverses the connections to take negative values as well, or uses meters with a suitable range.
7Repeat & meanRepeats each reading and calculates a mean current for each potential difference — write both halves as one phrase.
  • Swapping the ammeter and voltmeter round (ammeter in parallel) loses the Measure mark. Draw the circuit: it is credited ("a correct symbol for a variable resistor added in series with a lamp (1), ammeter in series (1), voltmeter in parallel (1)", June 2024 2H Q8(a)).
questions.hint: What do you put in the circuit to change the p.d.? Where does each meter go?

parts.intro: Write the full answer on paper, as seven numbered points, before you open the mark scheme. Then mark yourself against the rows — the question is levelled out of six, and a linked answer covering most of the seven rows is Level 3 (5–6).

checklist: Pick out the two variables a "describe a method" question is asking about
Name the formula or relationship that links them
Say which variable you change, how, and what you keep the same
Say which variable you measure, how, and with what equipment
Say what you will do with the results (a calculation or a graph)
Give one specific detail that makes the results accurate
Say you will repeat the readings and calculate a mean (both halves, or no mark)
sections.blurb: "Describe how you would investigate…" is worth six marks and most students get two. The same seven steps answer every version of it, in every topic.

sections.title: Evaluating a method: accuracy, precision and errors

parts.title: The words
parts.html:
WordMeansExample
AccurateClose to the true valueA balance reading 0.500 kg for a 500 g mass
PreciseRepeated readings are close to each other (small spread)0.512, 0.513, 0.512 kg — precise, but not accurate if the true value is 0.500 kg
ResolutionThe smallest change an instrument can showA millimetre rule has a resolution of 1 mm; a digital balance 0.01 g
RepeatableThe same person with the same equipment gets the same result againThree timings within 0.1 s of each other
ReproducibleA different person, or different equipment or method, gets the same resultAnother group's value for $g$ agrees with yours
ValidThe experiment actually tests what it claims to — only the independent variable was changedChanging the force without also changing the mass
Random errorScatter: readings vary unpredictably above and below the true valueReaction time on a stopwatch; reading a scale from slightly different angles
Systematic errorEvery reading is shifted the same wayA zero error on a balance; a rule with a worn end; a stopwatch that runs slow
Zero errorA systematic error where the instrument reads something when it should read zeroA newtonmeter that reads 0.2 N with nothing on it
Anomalous resultA reading much further from the mean than the other results — name the value, then give that reason (SAM Q4(b): "25.5 is anomalous (1) because it is much further away from the mean (1)")19.8, 20.1, 27.3, 20.0 s — the 27.3 s

parts.title: What fixes what
parts.html:
Repeating and taking a mean reduces the effect of random error, because the scatter above and below averages out. It does nothing for a systematic error — if the balance always reads 5 g high, the mean reads 5 g high too. Systematic errors are fixed by checking the zero, calibrating against a known value, or changing the method.

An anomalous result should be repeated if possible. If it cannot be, it is left out of the mean and circled on the graph — but you must say so.

"Human error" is never a creditworthy answer. Say what the error actually is: reaction time when starting the stopwatch, parallax when reading the rule, the thermometer not being at the same depth each time. Then the improvement with its reason — that is how "Explain one improvement" is marked: "use light gates (1) to eliminate reaction time (1)" (June 2018 1H Q6(c)); "use a longer distance (1) to give a more measurable time (1)" (June 2019 1H Q6(a)); "place the thermometer closer to the thermistor (1) so it measures the same temperature as the thermistor (1)" (June 2022 2H Q8(c)(i)). The reason can never be "more accurate" or "more precise" on its own — "do not accept more accurate without qualification"; "ignore accuracy, ignore precision". For a stopwatch the credited diagnosis is "reaction time is significant compared with the time measured". And in these questions "repeat and average" is ignored.

Higher resolution means a smaller uncertainty in each reading — a digital stopwatch (0.01 s) over a wall clock (1 s) — but it does not help if the reading is dominated by reaction time (about 0.2 s). Where the instrument is the limit — a thermometer in whole degrees, a rule in centimetres — "a thermometer with better resolution" and "a rule with millimetre divisions" are credited improvements (June 2022 2H Q8(c)(i), Nov 2020 2H Q6(a)(iii)).

parts.title: Evaluating a set of results
parts.question: A student times a pendulum's swing five times: 1.62 s, 1.58 s, 1.60 s, 1.91 s, 1.59 s. Her stopwatch has a resolution of 0.01 s. (a) Identify any anomalous result. (b) Calculate the mean. (c) Suggest one source of random error and how to reduce it. (d) Explain whether a stopwatch of resolution 0.001 s would improve the result.
steps: (a) 1.91 s is anomalous: it is far from the others, which are all within 0.04 s of each other.
(b) Leave it out: $\text{mean} = \dfrac{1.62 + 1.58 + 1.60 + 1.59}{4} = 1.60$ s (not divided by 5).

(c) Reaction time when starting and stopping the stopwatch — the student cannot press the button at exactly the end of a swing. Reduce it by timing ten swings and dividing by ten, so the reaction time is a smaller fraction of the measured time; or use a light gate.

(d) No. The reaction time (about 0.2 s) is much bigger than the resolution of either stopwatch, so a finer scale adds digits without adding accuracy. The limiting error is the method, not the instrument.

questions.text: A student's three readings of a resistance are 4.72 Ω, 4.71 Ω and 4.73 Ω. The true value is 5.00 Ω. The readings are:
questions.explain: The readings are close together (precise) but all well below the true value (not accurate) — the sign of a systematic error.

questions.text: Which of these is a systematic error?
options: Starting the stopwatch slightly late on some runs and slightly early on others
A balance that reads 2 g with nothing on the pan
Reading a ruler from different angles each time
Wind gusts affecting a falling object
questions.explain: A zero error shifts every reading the same way — systematic. The others vary from reading to reading: random.

questions.text: Explain the difference between a repeatable result and a reproducible result.
questions.model:
• Repeatable: the same experimenter, using the same method and equipment, gets the same (or very similar) result when they do it again.
  • Reproducible: a different experimenter, or a different method or equipment, gets the same result.

questions.text: A student measures the time for a ball to fall 2 m using a stopwatch and gets 0.74 s. Another student says "the error was human error". Explain why this is a poor evaluation, and give a better one.
questions.model:
• "Human error" does not say what went wrong or how to fix it, so it earns no credit.
  • The actual source is reaction time: the student cannot start and stop the stopwatch at exactly the right instants, which adds a random error of about 0.2 s to a fall of under a second.
  • Improvement: use a light gate or an electromagnetic release with an electronic timer, so the timing starts and stops automatically; or time a longer fall so the reaction time is a smaller fraction.

questions.text: Repeating readings and calculating a mean reduces the effect of:
questions.explain: Averaging cancels scatter — random error. A systematic shift is in every reading, so it survives the averaging unchanged.

questions.text: A student measures a spring's extension with a rule whose end is worn, so every length reads 2 mm too short. State the type of error, explain its effect on a graph of force against extension, and describe how to correct it.
questions.model:
• A systematic (zero) error.
  • Every extension would be wrong by the same amount — but extension is a difference of two lengths, so the 2 mm cancels; if instead the raw lengths were plotted, the whole line would shift and the intercept would be wrong while the gradient stayed correct.
  • Correct it by measuring from a clear mark (e.g. the 10 cm line) rather than the worn end, or by subtracting the zero error from each reading.

checklist: Define accuracy, precision, resolution, repeatable and reproducible
Tell a random error from a systematic error, and say what reduces each
Identify an anomalous result and say what to do with it
Explain why repeating and averaging improves a result (and what it does not fix)
sections.blurb: Accurate is not the same as precise, repeatable is not the same as reproducible, and "human error" is not an answer. The vocabulary is examined.

sections.title: Estimation questions

parts.title: How to answer an estimation question
parts.html:
An estimation question is marked on your method and sensible values, not on hitting one exact number. The examiner wants to see:

  1. Assumed values, written down with units — a mass, a speed, a time or distance.
  2. The equation you are using.
  3. The calculation, to 1 or 2 significant figures.
  4. A sense check: compare with something you know.
Useful values to know
Mass of an adult70 kg
Mass of a car1000–1500 kg
Height of a room / a floor of a building3 m
Height of a table0.8 m
Walking, running, cycling speed1.5, 3, 6 m/s
Car in town (30 mph), on a motorway (70 mph)13, 30 m/s
Power of a kettle, a car engine, a person2 kW, 100 kW, 100 W
Power of a phone charger, an LED lamp5 W, 10 W
Mass of an apple, a bag of sugar, a litre of water0.1 kg, 1 kg, 1 kg
Reaction time0.2–0.7 s
Speed of sound in air; speed of light340 m/s; $3 \times 10^8$ m/s

The schemes accept a range around the expected value (typically ±10–25%) once the read-off or substitution is shown; an unexplained number on its own is not enough for the method mark. Where you have had to assume a value, state it.

parts.title: Estimating an energy
parts.question: Estimate the work done by a student climbing one flight of stairs.
steps: Assume: mass $\approx 70$ kg; height of one floor $\approx 3$ m; $g = 10$ N/kg.
Work done against gravity $= $ gain in GPE $= m \times g \times h = 70 \times 10 \times 3 = 2100$ J.
Estimate: about $2000$ J (2 kJ).
Sense check: a chocolate bar stores about 1 MJ, so one flight of stairs is a tiny fraction of it — which matches experience.

questions.text: Estimate the weight of a family car.
questions.hint: Mass of a car ≈ 1000 kg; $W = m \times g$.

questions.text: Estimate the energy transferred by an electric heater left on for two hours.
questions.hint: A heater is about 2 kW; two hours in seconds.
walkthrough: $E = P \times t = 2000 \times 7200 \approx 1.4 \times 10^{7}$ J (about 14 MJ, or 4 kWh).

questions.text: Estimate the power of a student who runs up a flight of stairs in 3 s.
questions.hint: Work done ≈ 2100 J (from the worked example); divide by the time.
walkthrough: $P = \dfrac{E}{t} = \dfrac{2100}{3} = 700$ W — several times the 100 W a person sustains all day, which is why you cannot keep it up.

questions.text: Estimate the time it takes sound to travel the length of a football pitch.
questions.hint: A pitch is about 100 m; sound travels at 340 m/s.

questions.text: Describe how you would estimate the kinetic energy of a cyclist.
questions.model:
• State sensible assumed values: mass of cyclist plus bicycle about 80 kg; cycling speed about 6 m/s.
  • Use $KE = \tfrac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2$.
  • $KE \approx \tfrac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 6^2 \approx 1400$ J, given to 1 or 2 significant figures.
  • Sense-check it against a known value (e.g. a few times the energy to climb a step).

questions.text: Which is the best estimate of the height of a two-storey house?
questions.explain: Each floor is about 3 m, plus the roof: around 7 m. 30 m is a ten-storey block; 3 m is one floor.

checklist: Recall sensible everyday values: masses, speeds, times, heights, powers
State assumed values before using them
Give an estimate to one or two significant figures with a unit, and sense-check it
sections.blurb: "Estimate…" on an Edexcel paper means a calculation on approximate data the question gives you, or a value read off a graph, marked against a range (350–450 cm³ in June 2024 2H Q3(d); "any value that rounds to 2700" in June 2022 1H Q8(a)). Show the read-off or the substitution — it is the first mark. The sensible-values table below is for the rare question that gives you nothing, and for sense-checking every answer.

facts.a: kelvin, K (°C accepted where the question uses it)

facts.q: Unit of energy and work done?

facts.a: kilogram metre per second, kg m/s

facts.q: Which unit symbols take a capital letter?
facts.a: Those named after people: N, J, W, Pa, Hz, V, A, C, K, Ω

facts.q: Converting to a bigger unit makes the number…
Do leading zeros count as significant figures?
How many s.f. should an answer have?
facts.a: The same as the least precise data (usually 2 or 3); round only at the end — when the question asks for it, the rounding is its own mark, awarded for any value written to that many figures

facts.q: Standard form: the rule for the front number?

facts.a: weight ($W = m \times g$) or work done ($W = F \times d$)
charge ($Q = I \times t$) or thermal energy ($\Delta Q = m c \Delta \theta$)
power ($P = E \div t$) or pressure ($P = F \div A$)
take the square root of both sides

facts.q: Make $v$ the subject of $KE = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$
Make $t$ the subject of $a = (v - u) \div t$

facts.a: useful energy output ÷ total energy input (× 100 for %)
double one, double the other; straight line through the origin
double one, halve the other; $x \times y$ is constant
what happens, in order — no why
why, with reasons: because / so / therefore
a number with working and a unit (EWAU)
a value you get from the graph or data yourself
full working arriving at the value given
similarities and differences, mentioning both things

facts.q: "Discuss" wants… (Edexcel Physics says Discuss, not Evaluate)
facts.a: for and against (or the evidence on each side), then a justified conclusion
the evidence or reasoning for a given statement
a sensible physics idea applied to a new situation

facts.q: Which variable goes on the x-axis?
facts.a: The independent variable (the one you changed)
change in y ÷ change in x, from a large triangle on the line of best fit

facts.q: A line of best fit should…
facts.a: follow the trend with points balanced either side; not join the dots

facts.q: Straight line not through the origin is…
Seven steps to describe a practical?
facts.a: Two variables → formula → change (and keep same) → measure (equipment) → use the result → accuracy detail → repeat and calculate a mean
nothing — say "repeat and calculate a mean"
repeated readings are close to each other
the smallest change an instrument can show
Same person, same equipment, same result / different person or method, same result
Scatter above and below / every reading shifted the same way

facts.q: What to do with an anomalous result?
facts.a: Repeat it if you can; otherwise leave it out of the mean and say so

facts.q: Mass of an adult? of a car?
Power of a kettle? of a person?

facts.a: One kept the same so it does not affect the result
The range within which the true value is expected to lie
The instrument reads a non-zero value when it should read zero

factsBlurb: The whole topic on flip cards: every unit, every prefix, every command word. Cover, say the answer out loud, then flip to check.

types.name: Converting lengths, masses and times to SI units
types.method: Every equation on the sheet expects metres, kilograms and seconds, so convert before you substitute. Going from a small unit to a larger one (mm to m, g to kg) divides; going the other way multiplies. For areas and volumes, square or cube the length conversion: 1 m² is 100 × 100 cm² and 1 m³ is 100 × 100 × 100 cm³.
commonErrors: Multiplying when you should divide (120 cm is 1.2 m, not 12 000 m)
Converting hours to seconds by multiplying by 60 only once
Dividing cm² by 100 instead of by 10 000
Dividing cm³ by 100 or 1000 instead of by 1 000 000

worked.question: A bolt is 35 mm long. Convert this length to metres.
steps: Known: length = 35 mm. Unknown: length in m.
There are 1000 mm in 1 m, so divide by 1000.
Length = 0.035 m

practice.question: A desk is 120 cm wide. Convert this width to metres.
practice.hint: There are 100 cm in 1 m, so divide by 100.

practice.question: A packet of rice has a mass of 750 g. Convert this mass to kilograms.
practice.hint: There are 1000 g in 1 kg, so divide by 1000.

practice.question: A lorry carries 3.2 tonnes of gravel. 1 tonne = 1000 kg. Convert this mass to kilograms.
practice.hint: A tonne is bigger than a kilogram, so the number of kilograms must be bigger: multiply by 1000.

practice.question: A film lasts 2.5 hours. Convert this time to seconds.
practice.hint: Change hours to minutes first (× 60), then minutes to seconds (× 60 again).

practice.question: The front cover of a book has an area of 450 cm². Convert this area to m².
practice.hint: 1 m² is 100 cm × 100 cm = 10 000 cm², so divide by 10 000.

practice.question: A kettle holds 1500 cm³ of water. Convert this volume to m³.
practice.hint: 1 m³ is 100 cm × 100 cm × 100 cm = 1 000 000 cm³, so divide by 1 000 000.

types.name: Using prefixes: kilo, mega, giga, milli, micro, nano
types.method: A prefix in front of a unit is a multiplier. Kilo (k) means × 1000, mega (M) × 1 000 000 and giga (G) × 1 000 000 000. Milli (m) means ÷ 1000, micro (μ) ÷ 1 000 000 and nano (n) ÷ 1 000 000 000. Strip the prefix, apply the multiplier, and the value is in the base unit ready for the equation.
commonErrors: Mixing up milli (÷ 1000) and mega (× 1 000 000)
Treating a small prefix as a multiply: 20 mA is 0.02 A, not 20 000 A
Losing a zero in micro or nano: count the zeros, three per step
Leaving the prefix in and getting an answer 1000 times too big or too small

worked.question: A kettle transfers 540 kJ of energy to the water. Convert this energy to joules.
steps: Known: energy = 540 kJ. Unknown: energy in J.
kilo means × 1000.
Energy = 540 000 J

practice.question: The current through an LED is 20 mA. Convert this current to amps.
practice.hint: milli means ÷ 1000.

practice.question: A power station has an output of 1.8 GW. Convert this power to watts.
practice.hint: giga means × 1 000 000 000 (nine zeros).

practice.question: A wind turbine generates 2.5 MW on a windy day. Convert this power to watts.
practice.hint: mega means × 1 000 000 (six zeros).

practice.question: A resistor in a radio is labelled 4.7 kΩ. Convert this resistance to ohms.
practice.hint: kilo means × 1000, whatever the unit.

practice.question: A camera flash lasts 250 μs. Convert this time to seconds.
practice.hint: micro means ÷ 1 000 000 (six zeros).

practice.question: Red light has a wavelength of 650 nm. Convert this wavelength to metres.
practice.hint: nano means ÷ 1 000 000 000 (nine zeros).

types.name: Converting compound units: km/h, g/cm³ and kWh
types.method: A compound unit is two units combined, so convert each part in turn. For km/h to m/s, change the kilometres to metres (× 1000) and the hours to seconds (÷ 3600). For g/cm³ to kg/m³, change grams to kilograms (÷ 1000) and cm³ to m³ (÷ 1 000 000), which comes out as × 1000 overall. A kilowatt-hour is 1000 W for 3600 s, so 1 kWh = 3 600 000 J.
commonErrors: Converting the distance but forgetting the time (or the other way round)
Dividing by 3600 when going from m/s to km/h instead of multiplying
Using 1000 cm³ in a m³ instead of 1 000 000
Taking 1 kWh to be 1000 J or 3600 J

worked.question: A car travels at 90 km/h. Convert this speed to m/s.
steps: Known: speed = 90 km/h. Unknown: speed in m/s.
90 km in 1 hour is 90 × 1000 = 90 000 m in 3600 s.
Speed = 25 m/s

practice.question: A train travels at 108 km/h. Convert this speed to m/s.
practice.hint: Change km to m (× 1000) and hours to seconds (÷ 3600).

practice.question: A television uses 1.5 kWh of energy in a day. 1 kWh = 3 600 000 J. Convert this energy to joules.
practice.hint: Multiply the number of kWh by 3 600 000.

practice.question: A cyclist rides at 12 m/s. Convert this speed to km/h.
practice.hint: Work out how many metres are covered in one hour (3600 s), then change to km.
walkthrough: In 1 hour the cyclist covers 12 × 3600 = 43 200 m.

practice.question: Aluminium has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. Convert this density to kg/m³.
practice.hint: Change the grams to kilograms (÷ 1000) and the cm³ to m³ (÷ 1 000 000); a division in the bottom turns into a multiplication.

practice.question: A snail moves 15 cm in one minute. Calculate its speed in m/s.
practice.hint: Change 15 cm to metres and 1 minute to seconds before dividing.

practice.question: A bath tap delivers 12 litres of water per minute. 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Calculate the flow rate in m³/s.
practice.hint: Change 12 litres to cm³, then to m³ (÷ 1 000 000), then divide by 60 s.

types.name: Standard form for very large and very small values
equations: × 10ⁿ moves the decimal point n places to the right
× 10⁻ⁿ moves the decimal point n places to the left
types.method: Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ with a between 1 and 10. A positive power moves the decimal point to the right (a big number); a negative power moves it to the left (a small number). To write an ordinary number in standard form, count how many places the decimal point moves to leave one non-zero digit in front of it. Where a question asks for n, give the power alone; otherwise give the ordinary number.
commonErrors: Counting the zeros instead of the places the decimal point moves (2 500 000 is 2.5 × 10⁶, not 10⁵)
Dropping the minus sign on the power for a small number
Writing 25 × 10⁵ instead of 2.5 × 10⁶ (the front number must be less than 10)
Adding powers when you should be multiplying the front numbers too

worked.question: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 9.8 × 10⁷ Hz. Write this frequency as an ordinary number.
steps: Known: frequency = 9.8 × 10⁷ Hz. Unknown: the ordinary number.
The power is +7, so move the decimal point 7 places to the right.
9.8 → 98 000 000 (one place uses the 8, then six zeros)
Frequency = 98 000 000 Hz

practice.question: A microwave oven uses waves of wavelength 1.2 × 10⁻² m. Write this wavelength as an ordinary number.
practice.hint: A negative power moves the decimal point to the left: 2 places here.
walkthrough: Power is −2, so move the decimal point 2 places to the left.

practice.question: The radius of the Earth is 6.4 × 10⁶ m. Write this distance as an ordinary number.
practice.hint: A positive power moves the decimal point to the right: 6 places here.
walkthrough: Power is +6, so move the decimal point 6 places to the right.
6.4 → 6 400 000 (one place uses the 4, then five zeros)

practice.question: An ultrasound scanner uses a frequency of 2 500 000 Hz. In standard form this is 2.5 × 10ⁿ Hz. State the value of n.
practice.hint: Count how many places the decimal point moves from the end of 2 500 000 to sit after the 2.
walkthrough: Put the decimal point after the first digit: 2.5
From 2 500 000. to 2.5 the point moves 6 places to the left.

practice.question: Blue light has a wavelength of 0.000 000 45 m. In standard form this is 4.5 × 10ⁿ m. State the value of n.
practice.hint: The number is smaller than 1, so n is negative; count the places the point moves to the right to sit after the 4.
walkthrough: Put the decimal point after the first non-zero digit: 4.5
From 0.000 000 45 to 4.5 the point moves 7 places to the right.
A small number needs a negative power: 4.5 × 10⁻⁷

practice.question: A laser pulse lasts 2 × 10⁻⁶ s. Light travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Use distance = speed × time to calculate how far the pulse travels in that time. Give your answer as an ordinary number.
practice.hint: Multiply the front numbers (3 × 2) and add the powers (8 + (−6)), then write the result out in full.

practice.question: Each electron carries a charge of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. In one second 5 × 10¹⁹ electrons pass a point in a wire. Calculate the total charge that passes. Give your answer as an ordinary number.
practice.hint: Total charge = number of electrons × charge on one electron; multiply the front numbers and add the powers.

types.name: Rearranging an equation to find the unknown
types.method: Write the equation, list what you know, and circle the one quantity you do not. Undo whatever is being done to that quantity: a quantity that is multiplied is found by dividing, a quantity that is divided is found by multiplying, and a quantity that is squared is found by taking the square root last. Substitute only after rearranging, or substitute first and then solve, but keep the units with the numbers.
commonErrors: Dividing the wrong way round (I = V / P instead of I = P / V)
Forgetting to take the square root at the end when the unknown is squared
Taking the square root before dividing out the other quantities
Rearranging ρ = m / V to V = ρ / m instead of V = m / ρ

worked.question: A kettle has a power of 2300 W and is connected to the 230 V mains. Use P = I × V to calculate the current in the kettle.
steps: Known: P = 2300 W, V = 230 V. Unknown: I.
P = I × V → I = P / V
I = 10 A

practice.question: A sack of potatoes has a weight of 450 N. Use W = m × g to calculate its mass.
practice.hint: m is multiplied by g, so divide the weight by g = 10 N/kg.
walkthrough: W = 450 N, g = 10 N/kg, find m.
W = m × g → m = W / g

practice.question: Glass has a density of 2500 kg/m³. A glass block has a mass of 5 kg. Use ρ = m / V to calculate its volume.
practice.hint: V is on the bottom of the fraction: swap V and ρ so that V = m / ρ.
walkthrough: ρ = 2500 kg/m³, m = 5 kg, find V.
ρ = m / V → V = m / ρ

practice.question: A climber of mass 60 kg gains 3000 J of gravitational potential energy on a climbing wall. Use GPE = m × g × h to calculate the height climbed.
practice.hint: h is multiplied by both m and g, so divide the energy by m × g.
walkthrough: GPE = 3000 J, m = 60 kg, g = 10 N/kg, find h.
GPE = m × g × h → h = GPE / (m × g)

practice.question: A cyclist and bike of total mass 50 kg have 3600 J of kinetic energy. Use KE = ½ × m × v² to calculate the speed of the cyclist.
practice.hint: First find v² by doubling the energy and dividing by the mass; take the square root last.
walkthrough: KE = 3600 J, m = 50 kg, find v.
KE = ½ × m × v² → v² = 2 × KE / m

practice.question: A train accelerates at 2 m/s² over a distance of 200 m and reaches a velocity of 30 m/s. Use v² − u² = 2 × a × x to calculate its initial velocity.
practice.hint: Find u² first: u² = v² − 2 × a × x, then take the square root.
walkthrough: v = 30 m/s, a = 2 m/s², x = 200 m, find u.
v² − u² = 2 × a × x → u² = v² − 2 × a × x

practice.question: A spring with a spring constant of 50 N/m stores 1 J of elastic potential energy. Use E = ½ × k × x² to calculate its extension.
practice.hint: Find x² by doubling the energy and dividing by k, then take the square root.
walkthrough: E = 1 J, k = 50 N/m, find x.
E = ½ × k × x² → x² = 2 × E / k

types.name: Percentages and ratios in physics
equations: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input
types.method: A percentage is a fraction of the whole multiplied by 100. Efficiency is the useful output divided by the total input; multiply by 100 to give it as a percentage. For a percentage change, divide the change by the original value, not the new one. A ratio of two quantities is one divided by the other and has no unit.
commonErrors: Dividing the input by the output and getting an efficiency over 100%
Dividing a percentage change by the new value instead of the original
Forgetting to multiply by 100 when a percentage is asked for
Using the wasted energy as the useful output

worked.question: An electric motor is supplied with 500 J of energy and does 350 J of useful work lifting a load. Calculate the efficiency of the motor as a percentage.
steps: Known: useful output = 350 J, total input = 500 J. Unknown: efficiency.
efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input
efficiency = 350 / 500 = 0.7
As a percentage: 0.7 × 100 = 70%

practice.question: A kettle is supplied with 360 000 J of energy and transfers 324 000 J to the water. Calculate the efficiency of the kettle as a percentage.
practice.hint: Useful output divided by total input, then × 100.
walkthrough: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input

practice.question: A transformer has 400 turns on its primary coil and 50 turns on its secondary coil. Calculate the ratio of primary turns to secondary turns.
practice.hint: Divide the primary turns by the secondary turns; a ratio has no unit.

practice.question: A car's speed increases from 20 m/s to 25 m/s. Calculate the percentage increase in speed.
practice.hint: Find the change first, then divide by the original speed (20 m/s), not the new one.

practice.question: A litre of petrol stores 30 MJ of chemical energy. A car engine transfers 28% of this usefully. Calculate the useful energy transferred, in joules.
practice.hint: Change 30 MJ to joules first, then find 28% by multiplying by 0.28.

practice.question: An LED lamp has an input power of 12 W. It wastes 2.4 W as heat. Calculate the efficiency of the lamp as a percentage.
practice.hint: Find the useful power first by subtracting the wasted power from the input.
walkthrough: efficiency = useful power output / total power input

practice.question: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from a height of 2.0 m and bounces back up to a height of 1.4 m. Calculate the percentage of its gravitational potential energy that is lost in the bounce.
practice.hint: Work out the GPE at each height with GPE = m × g × h, find the energy lost, then divide by the original GPE and × 100.
